title: opentelemetry-event-sampler-and-heatmap-playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for adding a low-overhead OpenTelemetry-based event sampler to the serving runtime, and for turning sampled events into token-offset heatmaps and per-route hotpath visualizations. The goal is an always-on, low-cost signal to find performance hotspots in production without full-trace overhead.

Scope / motivation:
- We already have flamegraph and perf CI artifacts (separate docs). This focuses on: 1) sampling semantic events (model-start, kv-cache-hit, attention-kernel-run, memory-copy) and 2) producing compact visual artifacts (heatmaps of token positions vs latency, stacked bar hotpaths, event-rate timeseries).
- Useful for: regressions post-rollout, comparing quantized vs fp16 kernels, understanding per-sequence latencies, detecting token-position correlated slowdowns.

Design constraints:
- Production-safe: < 1% CPU overhead target at 10k qps; sampling fraction adjustable per-route.
- End-to-end trace IDs so a sampled event can be joined with logs and dashboards.
- Short payloads: event name, timestamp (ns), route, model_version, token_offset (if applicable), device, kernel_tag, cpu_ns, gpu_ms (if available).

High-level architecture:
1) Instrument runtime to emit Otel span events at key points: request-start, token-gen-start, kv-cache-lookup, attention-launch, kernel-queue, kernel-complete, response-end.
2) Sampler component (in-process) decides whether to keep event stream for this request (probabilistic or deterministic via traceid hashing).
3) Buffered export to a local agent (OTLP/gRPC or file) with batching and size limits.
4) Collector pipeline (central) that performs: enrichment (map kernel_tag->kernel_version), dedupe, token-offset bucketing, and heatmap generation.
5) Storage of compressed artifacts (parquet or ndjson) and PNG/SVG heatmaps uploaded to artifact storage (S3/GCS) and linked in dashboards.

Sampling strategy notes:
- Deterministic sampling by traceid modulo N: ensures even spread and reproducible picks per trace. Good for A/B compare across deployments.
- Adaptive burst sampling: sample first M requests per route per minute at 100% then drop to baseline fraction. Helps capture rollout transition effects.
- Rate-limited sampling for heavy routes to avoid explosion when traffic spikes.

Event schema (minimal):
- trace_id: hex
- span_id: hex
- ts_ns: integer string
- event: string (see below)
- route: string
- model: string
- model_version: string
- token_offset: integer string (nullable)
- stage: string (e.g., "kv", "attn", "decode")
- kernel_tag: string (nullable)
- device: string (e.g., "cuda:0")
- cpu_ms: float string (optional)
- gpu_ms: float string (optional)
- notes: string (optional)

Key events to emit (suggested names):
- request.start
- request.queue_enter
- request.queue_exit
- generation.token.start
- generation.token.end
- kv.lookup.start
- kv.lookup.end
- kernel.launch
- kernel.complete
- response.finish

Practical instrumentation tips:
- Emit token_offset only during generation.token.* events. For batch decode where offsets are not explicit, use relative-token-index within request.
- Avoid synchronous allocations in hot paths; write to a pre-allocated fixed-size ring buffer and let a background thread serialize batches.
- Use lightweight integer enum mapping for event names on wire when using binary exporter.

Collector pipeline prototype (commands):
- Start a small local collector for dev:
  docker run --rm -p 4317:4317 otel/opentelemetry-collector:latest \
    --config /etc/otel/collector-config.yaml

- Simple receiver config (dev):
  receivers:
    otlp:
      protocols:
        grpc: {}
  exporters:
    file/trace:
      path: /tmp/otel-traces.jsonl
  service:
    pipelines:
      traces:
        receivers: [otlp]
        exporters: [file/trace]

Post-processing example (python sketch):
  1) read /tmp/otel-traces.jsonl (ndjson)
  2) for each trace: build list of events, compute per-token latency = token_end - token_start
  3) bucket token_offset into 0..N (e.g., 0-15,16-63,64-255) and accumulate latency stats
  4) produce matrix rows=token_bucket x cols=route/model, value=95th latency
  5) render heatmap via matplotlib and save SVG

CI job idea (perf sampling job):
- Trigger: nightly on serving-runtime main and after every canary rollout.
- Steps:
  1) Deploy a small test fleet (k3s or lightweight cluster) pinned to a candidate commit.
  2) Replay traffic using production-like prompt corpus (sampled prompts JSON).
  3) Enable deterministic sampling at 1% and adaptive burst for first 1000 requests.
  4) Collect OTLP export file and artifacts, run post-processor to create heatmaps and token-latency histograms.
  5) Upload artifacts to build storage and annotate the PR with links.
- Failure conditions: if 95th token-latency in any bucket increases > X ms vs baseline, mark job failed (X configurable, default 30ms).

Implementation pitfalls and mitigations:
- High-cardinality route names: normalize route to pattern rather than full user id. Use hashing for any sensitive data.
- Very long sequences: cap token_offset recording for first 1024 tokens to bound matrix size. Export tail-sampled summaries for longer sequences.
- GPU time attribution: sometimes kernel complete -> next kernel launch has overlap; prefer to use kernel-level timestamps when available (driver GPU timers) rather than wall-clock.

Visualization recommendations:
- Heatmap: x-axis token buckets, y-axis routes or model_versions. Color = 95th lat. Use log color scale for better spread.
- Stacked timeline: show event stages per token to spot where time accrues (queue vs kv vs kernel).
- Sparklines per route for sampled trace-rate and average payload size.

On-call runbook snippets (quick steps to run when investigating a reported regression):
1) Check the sampling artifact dashboard for the rollout window. Filter by route and model_version.
2) Open corresponding heatmap SVG and inspect token buckets for spikes.
3) If spike concentrated in kernel stage: pull kernel_tag distribution from events and map to GPU driver logs.
4) If spike in kv stage: check Redis/memstore latency metrics correlated by route.
5) For ambiguous cases: fetch raw traces for 10 sampled trace_ids and run full flamegraph using existing perf pipeline.

Small example: shell commands to generate a quick local artifact
  # start local collector
  docker run --rm -p 4317:4317 otel/opentelemetry-collector:latest --config ./dev-collector.yaml &
  # run a short load replay with deterministic sampling via env
  SAMPLING_STRATEGY=deterministic SAMPLING_MOD=100 ./tools/replay_production_prompts.sh --duration 60s --concurrency 8 --otlp-endpoint localhost:4317
  # once file generated
  python tools/otel_heatmap_postproc.py --input /tmp/otel-traces.jsonl --out artifacts/heatmap.svg

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide canonical token_bucket boundaries (power-of-two vs linear).
- Add secure sampling mode for regulated customers where event payload must be PII-free.
- Integrate with console rollout page: show latest heatmap per canary and diff vs baseline.
- Explore minimal on-device summarization (compute per-shard aggregates in GPU host to reduce export bandwidth).

Appendix: quick json example of a single event line (ndjson):
{
  "trace_id": "a1b2c3d4e5f6",
  "span_id": "11aa22bb",
  "ts_ns": "1710001234567890",
  "event": "generation.token.end",
  "route": "/api/v1/generate",
  "model": "redwood-llama-13b",
  "model_version": "2024-05-01-quant",
  "token_offset": "42",
  "stage": "decode",
  "kernel_tag": "matmul_v2_quant",
  "device": "cuda:2",
  "cpu_ms": "0.12",
  "gpu_ms": "1.8"
}

End of playbook (working draft).
